title: Create a local Kubernetes cluster with kind
description: From nothing to a running multi-node cluster: install the tools, create local-cluster-1, switch kubectl to it, make namespaces.
html:
From nothing to a running multi-node cluster with namespaces ready for your apps: install the tools, create the cluster local-cluster-1, switch kubectl to it, look at the nodes, make namespaces. Every command is here, one per line, with what it does and what you should see. Nothing depends on a script: you type (or paste) each command yourself.

New to the words (node, context, namespace)? Read Concepts: what each piece is first, or alongside.

Two habits that save time

  • Paste one command at a time. Long lines sometimes wrap in the terminal and run as two broken halves. Every command below is kept short for that reason.
  • Run the check at the end of each part before moving on. If the output differs, stop and re-check the previous command before going further.

The names used throughout (change them if you like, but change them everywhere):

ThingName
Clusterlocal-cluster-1
kubectl contextkind-local-cluster-1 (kind always adds the kind- prefix)
Nodeslocal-cluster-1-control-plane, local-cluster-1-worker, local-cluster-1-worker2
Namespacesweb, cache, db

#Part 1 — Prepare the machine

1.1 Start Docker. kind runs every Kubernetes node as a Docker container, so Docker must be running. Open Docker Desktop and wait until it says it is running, then:

Prints a version number (for example 29.8.2). An error like "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon" means Docker is not up yet.

1.2 Give Docker enough memory. Docker Desktop → Settings → Resources. Three nodes need roughly 4 GB or more; 8 GB is comfortable. Apply & restart, then check what Docker actually has:

A number in bytes (8000000000 ≈ 8 GB).

1.3 Install the tools (macOS with Homebrew):

  • kind — creates and deletes the cluster.
  • kubectl — the command you use to talk to any Kubernetes cluster. (Docker Desktop may already provide one; if kubectl version --client works you can skip this.)

Check:

Both print a version. Nothing else is needed for this guide.

#Part 2 — Create the cluster

2.1 Write the cluster description. kind builds whatever a small YAML file describes. This one asks for one control-plane node and two worker nodes:

Line by line:

  • name: local-cluster-1 — the cluster's name. It becomes the prefix of the node containers and the suffix of the kubectl context.
  • role: control-plane — the "brain" node: API server, scheduler, etcd.
  • role: worker (twice) — nodes that run your pods. Two lines, two workers.
  • extraPortMappings — opens a door from your Mac into the cluster: Mac port 8080 → port 30080 on the node. It is used in Part 2.3 of Deploy apps into your namespaces, one at a time. It can only be set now, when the cluster is created.

kind cannot add a node to a running cluster. To change the number of nodes, edit this file, delete the cluster (Stop, shut down and clean up) and create it again. That takes about a minute, so experiment freely.

2.2 Create it (one to two minutes the first time: kind downloads a node image of about 1 GB):

It prints a checklist (Preparing nodes, Writing configuration, Starting control-plane, Joining worker nodes…) and ends with Set kubectl context to "kind-local-cluster-1".

2.3 Look at what Docker now has. Each node is one container:

And kind's own view:

Check: kind get clusters lists local-cluster-1, and three node containers are Up.

#Part 3 — Switch to the cluster

kubectl keeps a list of clusters it can talk to (the kubeconfig, ~/.kube/config). Each entry is a context: a cluster plus a user. Every kubectl command goes to the current context.

Why this part matters. If your kubeconfig also holds a cloud or work cluster, a command meant for your toy cluster will happily run against that one. Always know the current context.

3.1 List the contexts (* marks the current one):

You should see kind-local-cluster-1 in the list.

3.2 Show just the current one:

kind create cluster already switched to the new cluster, so this normally prints kind-local-cluster-1.

3.3 Switch to it explicitly (what you run any time the current context is something else):

Prints Switched to context "kind-local-cluster-1".

3.4 Confirm it answers:

Prints the API server address (https://127.0.0.1:<random port>) and CoreDNS.

3.5 A safety habit. Add --context to a single command to aim it without switching:

Check: kubectl config current-context prints kind-local-cluster-1.

#Part 4 — The nodes

4.1 See them:

All three must be Ready. (ROLES <none> on a worker is normal.)

4.2 More detail: internal IPs, OS, container runtime:

4.3 Label the workers. A label is a sticky note on an object. On its own it does nothing; it only matters when a pod asks for it. In Part 1.3 of Deploy apps into your namespaces, one at a time the Postgres pod says nodeSelector: role: data ("run me only on a node labelled role=data"), so the scheduler puts it on the node labelled that way. A pod with no nodeSelector can land on any worker. These two labels set up that choice; role=app is not used until you write a pod that selects it:

Check:

The two workers show role=app and role=data among their labels.

4.4 Why pods never land on the control-plane. A label lets a pod choose a node. A taint works the other way round: it is a "keep out" sign on the node. The scheduler (the part that picks a node for each pod) will not place a pod on a tainted node unless the pod carries a matching permission slip, called a toleration.

A taint is written key=value:effect:

PartHereMeaning
keynode-role.kubernetes.io/control-planethe name of the taint
value(empty)not needed, the key says it all
effectNoSchedulewhat the taint does

The three effects:

  • NoSchedule — new pods without a toleration are not placed here. Pods already running stay.
  • PreferNoSchedule — a soft version: avoided, but used if nothing else fits.
  • NoExecute — also evicts pods already running there that do not tolerate it.

Why the control-plane has one. It runs the cluster's brain (API server, scheduler, etcd). If your apps shared the node and used up its CPU or memory, the whole cluster could slow down or stop answering. The cluster's own components carry the toleration, so they can run there. Your pods do not, so they only run on the workers.

A single-node cluster is different. With only a control-plane node, kind removes this taint, because there would be nowhere else to run pods. The taint is present in this 3-node config, not always.

Running a pod on the control-plane anyway. Give the pod a toleration:

Each field says how to match a taint:

  • key — which taint this toleration is for.
  • effect — which effect it covers. Leave it out and it covers every effect of that key.
  • operator — how the key (and value) are compared. Table below.
operatorMatches whenvalue
Existsthe node has a taint with that key, whatever its valueleave it out
Equal (the default)the key and the value are both the samerequired

Exists fits here because the control-plane taint has no value. Equal fits a taint that has one, such as dedicated=data:NoSchedule: the toleration then says key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: data. An Exists toleration with no key at all matches every taint, a pass for the whole cluster; use it only for system components.

A toleration is permission, not a command. It lets a pod onto a tainted node but does not send it there. To send it, add a nodeSelector as well.

Or remove the taint from the node. The trailing - means "delete this taint":

Not something to do routinely; it is mainly useful on very small clusters.

#Part 5 — Namespaces

A namespace is a folder inside the cluster. Names only have to be unique within one, and you can look at one folder at a time. Create the three used below:

Check:

web, cache and db are there, next to the built-in default, kube-system, kube-public and kube-node-lease.

Every later command carries -n <namespace> to say which folder it means. Leave it off and kubectl uses default. (To change that default for the current context: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=web. This guide always spells out -n, so you can skip it.)
